Why pseudohaploids must be declared

Source: vignettes/articles/pseudohaploids.Rmd
pseudohaploids.Rmd

Diploid genotypes cannot be called reliably from low-coverage data, which includes most ancient genomes. A common workaround is to sample a single allele at random at each site, so that the individual is treated as “pseudohaploid”. tidypopgen encodes each pseudohaploid call as a homozygous genotype (0 or 2), and tidypopgen::gt_pseudohaploid() marks the individuals with no heterozygous genotypes as pseudohaploids (with a ploidy of 1). gt_radmix() estimates ancestry proportions with the method and the algorithm of ADMIXTURE (Alexander et al. 2009), including its cross-validation procedure (Alexander & Lange 2011). For pseudohaploid individuals, it counts a single copy of the allele at each genotype.

If the pseudohaploid individuals are not declared as such, each genotype is treated as a true diploid call. This happens in programs such as ADMIXTURE, which assume diploid genotypes for autosomes. Using simulated data, we show below the consequences of this approach. In summary, we show that:

  • the log-likelihood of every pseudohaploid is doubled. Likelihood-based criteria for choosing K (such as the Akaike information criterion, AIC) tend to favour an increasing number of clusters, whereas cross-validation generally identifies the correct K;
  • when the population structure is weak, cross-validation can support too few clusters;
  • even at the correct K, diploid individuals from the population containing pseudohaploid individuals appear artificially admixed;
  • when K is too large, the additional clusters artificially divide the pseudohaploid individuals into groups that do not reflect genuine population structure.

All of these artefacts disappear once the pseudohaploids are declared with gt_pseudohaploid().

The first sections analyse a single simulated dataset, with code that runs in a few seconds. The later sections summarise replicated simulations, run with a script described in How the replicated simulations were run.

Simulating the data

First, we load the packages required for the simulations and subsequent analyses.

library(tidygenclust)
library(tidypopgen)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

The simulations follow the ADMIXTURE model, with unadmixed individuals from a few populations:

  1. For each of n_loci independent loci, the frequency of the alternate allele is drawn from a uniform distribution between 0.05 and 0.95 in a common ancestral population.
  2. Each population drifts from the ancestral population: the alternative allele frequency of each locus is drawn independently for each population from the Balding-Nichols model (Balding & Nichols 1995), a beta distribution with the ancestral frequency p as its mean and a variance of fst * p * (1 - p). The larger fst is, the more the populations differ.
  3. Each diploid individual carries two independently sampled alleles at each locus, with the probability of sampling the alternate allele given by its population-specific frequency. The resulting genotype therefore follows a binomial distribution with two trials, and takes the values 0, 1 or 2.
  4. Each pseudohaploid individual carries a single sampled allele at each locus, drawn according to the population-specific allele frequency. This mimics the random selection of a single allele at each site: At a heterozygous site, either allele is equally likely to be selected. Consequently, across individuals, the probability of observing the alternate allele is equal to its population frequency. The genotype is stored as 0 or 2.

The simulated data contain no missing genotypes, no linkage between loci and no admixture, so the true number of clusters equals the number of populations. The function simulate_pseudohaploids() implements these steps. The populations and their numbers of diploid and pseudohaploid individuals are given as named vectors. It returns a gen_tibble in which the pseudohaploids are coded 0/2 but not declared, as when they are read from a file (with the true allele frequencies of the populations in its attribute “frequencies”):

# Simulate diploid and pseudohaploid individuals from a few populations.
# n_diploid and n_pseudohaploid are named vectors with the number of
# individuals of each population (a population missing from one of them has
# none of that type), e.g. n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 20) and
# n_pseudohaploid = c(A = 40). The allele frequencies of each population
# drift from those of a common ancestral population (with the given F_ST).
# Returns a gen_tibble with the columns id, population and type ("diploid" or
# "pseudohaploid"), in which the pseudohaploids are coded 0/2 but not
# declared as pseudohaploids, as when they are read from a file. The true
# allele frequencies of the populations (a matrix with one row per locus and
# one column per population) are in its attribute "frequencies"
simulate_pseudohaploids <- function(n_diploid, n_pseudohaploid = c(),
                                    n_loci = 5000, fst = 0.1, seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) {
    set.seed(seed)
  }
  populations <- union(names(n_diploid), names(n_pseudohaploid))
  # the number of individuals of a population in n (0 if it is not in n)
  count <- function(n, pop) if (pop %in% names(n)) n[[pop]] else 0
  # the frequency of the alternate allele of each locus in the ancestral
  # population
  p_ancestral <- stats::runif(n_loci, 0.05, 0.95)
  frequencies <- list()
  genotypes <- list()
  indiv_meta <- list()
  for (pop in populations) {
    # the frequencies in this population, drifted from the ancestral ones
    # (Balding-Nichols model: a beta distribution with mean p_ancestral and
    # variance fst * p_ancestral * (1 - p_ancestral))
    p_pop <- frequencies[[pop]] <- stats::rbeta(
      n_loci,
      p_ancestral * (1 - fst) / fst,
      (1 - p_ancestral) * (1 - fst) / fst
    )
    # n individuals with `copies` copies of each locus, each copy carrying
    # the alternate allele with probability p_pop (one row per individual)
    draw <- function(n, copies) {
      matrix(
        stats::rbinom(n * n_loci, copies, p_pop),
        ncol = n_loci, byrow = TRUE
      )
    }
    # a diploid carries two copies; a pseudohaploid carries one, stored as a
    # homozygous genotype (0 or 2), as in tidypopgen
    n_dip <- count(n_diploid, pop)
    n_pseudo <- count(n_pseudohaploid, pop)
    genotypes[[pop]] <- rbind(draw(n_dip, 2), 2 * draw(n_pseudo, 1))
    indiv_meta[[pop]] <- data.frame(
      population = rep(pop, n_dip + n_pseudo),
      type = rep(c("diploid", "pseudohaploid"), c(n_dip, n_pseudo))
    )
  }
  indiv_meta <- do.call(rbind, indiv_meta)
  indiv_meta <- data.frame(
    id = paste0("ind", seq_len(nrow(indiv_meta))),
    indiv_meta
  )
  loci <- data.frame(
    name = paste0("rs", seq_len(n_loci)),
    chromosome = 1L,
    position = seq_len(n_loci),
    genetic_dist = 0,
    allele_ref = "A",
    allele_alt = "T"
  )
  gt <- tidypopgen::gen_tibble(
    do.call(rbind, genotypes),
    indiv_meta = indiv_meta,
    loci = loci,
    backingfile = tempfile("pseudohaploids_"),
    quiet = TRUE
  )
  attr(gt, "frequencies") <- do.call(cbind, frequencies)
  gt
}

The function is defined in vignettes/articles/code/pseudohaploid_simulation.R (in the source code of the package), and can be loaded with source() to simulate other designs.

As a first example, we simulate two populations, A and B, that have each diverged from their common ancestor with an F_ST of 0.1. The dataset comprises 5,000 loci, 20 diploid individuals from each of populations A and B, and an additional 40 pseudohaploid individuals from population A.

gt <- simulate_pseudohaploids(
  n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 20),
  n_pseudohaploid = c(A = 40),
  fst = 0.1,
  seed = 1
)
gt
#> # A gen_tibble: 5000 loci
#> # A tibble:     80 × 4
#>    id    population type     genotypes
#>    <chr> <chr>      <chr>   <vctr_SNP>
#>  1 ind1  A          diploid  [0,1,...]
#>  2 ind2  A          diploid  [0,0,...]
#>  3 ind3  A          diploid  [0,0,...]
#>  4 ind4  A          diploid  [1,0,...]
#>  5 ind5  A          diploid  [0,2,...]
#>  6 ind6  A          diploid  [0,0,...]
#>  7 ind7  A          diploid  [0,1,...]
#>  8 ind8  A          diploid  [0,1,...]
#>  9 ind9  A          diploid  [0,1,...]
#> 10 ind10 A          diploid  [0,1,...]
#> # ℹ 70 more rows
table(gt$population, gt$type)
#>    
#>     diploid pseudohaploid
#>   A      20            40
#>   B      20             0

The pseudohaploids have no heterozygous genotypes:

heterozygosity <- rowMeans(show_genotypes(gt) == 1)
tapply(heterozygosity, gt$type, mean)
#>       diploid pseudohaploid 
#>      0.323615      0.000000

The function gt_pseudohaploid() identifies them:

gt_declared <- gt_pseudohaploid(gt)
table(type = gt$type, ploidy = indiv_ploidy(gt_declared))
#>                ploidy
#> type             1  2
#>   diploid        0 40
#>   pseudohaploid 40  0

The log-likelihood counts the pseudohaploids twice

We fit the true model (K = 2) twice: once with the pseudohaploids treated as diploids (undeclared), and once with them declared:

fit_undeclared <- gt_radmix(gt, k = 2, seed = 1)
fit_declared <- gt_radmix(gt_declared, k = 2, seed = 1)
c(undeclared = fit_undeclared$loglik, declared = fit_declared$loglik)
#> undeclared   declared 
#>  -382540.8  -286929.4

The two log-likelihoods are very different. In the ADMIXTURE model, the genotype g at a given locus is the number of alternate-allele copies carried by an individual, out of n total allele copies. The number of alternate-allele copies follows a binomial distribution with n trials and a probability of observing the alternate allele given by qp = sum_k q_k p_k (where q_k is the proportion of the ancestry of the individual from cluster k, and p_k the frequency of the allele in that cluster). The log-likelihood contribution of this genotype is therefore

g log(qp) + (n - g) log(1 - qp)

A declared pseudohaploid individual carrying the alternate allele at a locus has g = 1 out of n = 1, and contributes log(qp). Undeclared, it has g = 2 out of n = 2, and contributes 2 log(qp). The same holds for the reference allele: g = 0 contributes log(1 - qp) when declared and 2 log(1 - qp) when undeclared. The log-likelihood of every pseudohaploid is therefore exactly doubled. We can check this by computing the log-likelihood of each individual from the estimates of the declared fit:

# the log-likelihood of each individual, given the genotypes `gt`, the
# ancestry proportions q (individuals x K), the allele frequencies p
# (loci x K) and the number of allele copies of each individual
loglik_individuals <- function(gt, q, p, n_copies) {
  # copies of the alternate allele out of n_copies (the pseudohaploids are
  # coded 0/2)
  copies <- show_genotypes(gt) * n_copies / 2
  qp <- q %*% t(p)
  rowSums(copies * log(qp) + (n_copies - copies) * log(1 - qp))
}
q <- unclass(fit_declared$Q[[1]])
p <- fit_declared$P[[1]]
loglik_declared <- loglik_individuals(gt, q, p, indiv_ploidy(gt_declared))
loglik_undeclared <- loglik_individuals(gt, q, p, n_copies = 2)
# the total for the declared pseudohaploids is that of the fit
c(by_hand = sum(loglik_declared), fit = fit_declared$loglik)
#>   by_hand       fit 
#> -286929.4 -286929.4
# the log-likelihood of each type of individual, with the same estimates
rbind(
  declared = tapply(loglik_declared, gt$type, sum),
  undeclared = tapply(loglik_undeclared, gt$type, sum)
)
#>              diploid pseudohaploid
#> declared   -190883.8     -96045.62
#> undeclared -190883.8    -192091.24

The diploids contribute the same log-likelihood in both cases, but the pseudohaploids contribute twice as much when undeclared. The model behaves as if it had twice as much information about the pseudohaploids as it really has. The rest of this article shows the consequences.

Ancestry proportions at the true K

Given the allele frequencies, the ancestry proportions of the pseudohaploids maximise their own log-likelihood, and doubling that log-likelihood does not change where the maximum is. However, the pseudohaploids also affect the allele frequencies of the clusters, and through them the ancestry of the other individuals:

# the ancestry proportions of a gt_admix object with a single run, as a
# data frame with one row per individual and cluster, labelled with the
# treatment ("declared" or "undeclared")

q_long <- function(fit, gt, treatment) {
  q <- unclass(fit$Q[[1]])
  data.frame(
    treatment = treatment,
    k = fit$k,
    id = gt$id,
    population = gt$population,
    type = gt$type,
    cluster = rep(seq_len(ncol(q)), each = nrow(q)),
    q = as.vector(q)
  )
}
# one colour per cluster (from the Okabe-Ito palette); the numbering of the
# clusters, and hence their colours, is arbitrary in each fit
cluster_colours <- c(
  "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442", "#0072B2", "#D55E00"
)
# bar plot of the ancestry proportions of each individual (from q_long()),
# with one row of panels per K and per treatment, and the individuals
# grouped by population and type, and sorted within each group by their
# ancestry from the main cluster of the group
plot_q <- function(q) {
  # one row of panels per K and treatment, undeclared first
  rows <- paste0(
    "K = ", rep(sort(unique(q$k)), each = 2), "\n",
    c("undeclared", "declared")
  )
  q <- q %>%
    mutate(
      group = paste0(.data$population, "\n(", .data$type, ")"),
      row = factor(paste0("K = ", .data$k, "\n", .data$treatment), rows)
    ) %>%
    group_by(.data$treatment, .data$k, .data$group, .data$cluster) %>%
    mutate(cluster_mean = mean(.data$q)) %>%
    group_by(.data$treatment, .data$k, .data$group) %>%
    mutate(
      main_cluster = .data$cluster[which.max(.data$cluster_mean)]
    ) %>%
    group_by(.data$treatment, .data$k, .data$id) %>%
    mutate(main_q = .data$q[.data$cluster == .data$main_cluster[1]]) %>%
    group_by(.data$treatment, .data$k) %>%
    arrange(.data$group, desc(.data$main_q), .data$id, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(individual = match(.data$id, unique(.data$id))) %>%
    ungroup()
  ggplot(q, aes(
    x = .data$individual, y = .data$q, fill = factor(.data$cluster)
  )) +
    geom_col(width = 1) +
    facet_grid(
      row ~ group,
      scales = "free_x",
      space = "free_x"
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colours, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = NULL, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      panel.spacing = unit(0.2, "lines"),
      strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0)
    )
}
plot_q(rbind(
  q_long(fit_undeclared, gt, "undeclared"),
  q_long(fit_declared, gt, "declared")
))

Declared, every individual is assigned almost entirely to the cluster of its population. A few individuals of A get a little ancestry from the cluster of B, and none of B from that of A, but this is due to the larger sample of A (60 individuals against 20), not to its pseudohaploids (see Why population A looks slightly admixed). Undeclared, the pseudohaploids are still assigned to their own cluster, but the diploids of population A appear slightly admixed with population B. Treated as diploids, the pseudohaploids are homozygous at every locus, which the model can only partly explain, with allele frequencies closer to 0 and 1. As they make up most of the information on population A (counted twice, they carry 80 of its 120 allele copies per locus), the cluster of population A takes more extreme frequencies than the true frequencies of the population. The diploids of population A, which do carry heterozygotes, then fit better as a mixture of this cluster with that of population B.

The replicated simulations (see Choosing K for their design) show the same bias, which is stronger when the structure is weak. The table gives the mean ancestry of each group of individuals from the cluster of the other population, at K = 2:

Mean ancestry (%) of each group of individuals from the cluster of the other population at K = 2, over 5 replicates.
Scenario Population Type Undeclared (%) Declared (%)
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.1 A diploid 5.3 1.0
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.1 A pseudohaploid 1.2 1.3
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.1 B diploid 0.2 0.3
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.05 A diploid 12.4 3.1
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.05 A pseudohaploid 3.3 3.0
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.05 B diploid 1.0 1.1
B only pseudohaploids, F_ST = 0.1 A diploid 0.2 0.2
B only pseudohaploids, F_ST = 0.1 B pseudohaploid 0.9 0.7

When undeclared, the pseudohaploids make the diploids of their population appear four to five times more admixed than when they are declared. The pseudohaploids themselves, and the other population, are almost unaffected. There is no bias when one population is made up only of pseudohaploids (the third scenario), as there are no diploids in it to appear admixed.

Even when the pseudohaploids are declared, the individuals of population A get a little more ancestry from the other cluster than those of B do. As explained below, this is not due to the pseudohaploids.

Why population A looks slightly admixed

The ancestry of an individual is estimated from a finite number of loci, and cannot be negative, so the noise of the estimate shows up as a little ancestry from the other cluster, even in an unadmixed individual. In the scenarios above, this is larger in population A than in B. Two differences between the populations could explain this: A has more individuals (60 against 20), and two thirds of them are pseudohaploids, whose ancestry is estimated with more noise. To separate the two, we simulated two populations of different or equal sizes, with and without pseudohaploids (F_ST = 0.1, 10 replicates). We fitted K = 2 in two ways: with the allele frequencies estimated, as usual, and with them fixed at their true values (stored in the “frequencies” of the simulated data, and passed to gt_radmix() with init_p and fix_p = TRUE):

Mean ancestry (%) of each group of individuals from the cluster of the other population at K = 2, over 10 replicates, with the allele frequencies estimated (with the pseudohaploids undeclared or declared), or fixed at their true values.
Simulated individuals Population Type Undeclared (%) Declared (%) Declared, true frequencies (%)
A: 20 diploids; B: 20 diploids A diploid - 0.2 0.6
B diploid - 0.3 0.6
A: 60 diploids; B: 20 diploids A diploid - 1.1 0.6
B diploid - 0.3 0.7
A: 20 diploids and 40 pseudohaploids; B: 20 diploids (the first scenario) A diploid 5.1 1.1 0.6
A pseudohaploid 1.2 1.5 0.9
B diploid 0.2 0.2 0.7
A: 20 diploids and 40 pseudohaploids; B: 60 diploids A diploid 4.7 1.0 0.6
A pseudohaploid 1.0 1.3 0.9
B diploid 0.9 0.9 0.6
  • With the true frequencies, all diploids get about the same small ancestry from the other cluster (0.6% on average), whatever the size of their population: this is the noise of the estimates. The pseudohaploids, with half as many allele copies, get a little more (0.9%).
  • With the estimated frequencies, the difference between the populations follows their sizes, not the pseudohaploids. Without any pseudohaploids, A (60 diploids) still looks more admixed than B (20 diploids), by about the same amount as in the original scenario (A: 20 diploids and 40 pseudohaploids; B: 20 diploids). Conversely, when the pseudohaploids are kept in A but B is enlarged to 60 diploids, the two populations look alike. The allele frequencies of a cluster are estimated from the individuals assigned to it. With few individuals, the estimated frequencies are pulled towards each of them and fit them closely, so they appear less admixed than with the true frequencies (as in B, with 20 individuals). With many, each individual has less influence on the frequencies, which fit them less closely, so they appear more admixed (as in A, with 60).
  • The pseudohaploids themselves appear a little more admixed than the diploids of their population, because of the larger noise of their estimates.
  • Undeclared pseudohaploids add a much larger bias to the diploids of A, which remains when B is as large as A: it comes from the extreme frequencies of the cluster of A, explained above, not from the sizes of the populations.

So, when the pseudohaploids are declared, the slight admixture of population A comes mostly from its larger sample, and only a little from its pseudohaploids. It is a property of the maximum-likelihood estimates of the ADMIXTURE model, with or without pseudohaploids, and the differences are small (about 1%).

Choosing K

The replicated simulations have 5 replicates of each of three scenarios, each with two populations (so the true K is 2), and 5,000 loci:

  • Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.1: as above, 20 diploids from each population, and 40 pseudohaploids from population A;
  • Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.05: the same, with weaker structure;
  • Pseudohaploids in B only, F_ST = 0.1: 20 diploids from population A, and 40 pseudohaploids from population B, e.g. a population known only from ancient samples.

Each dataset is analysed with gt_radmix() for K = 1 to 6, with cross-validation, with its pseudohaploids undeclared and declared.

The log-likelihood keeps adding clusters

Adding a cluster always increases the log-likelihood, as the extra parameters can fit some of the noise of the sample. Criteria based on the log-likelihood, such as AIC, only add a cluster if the increase is large enough. AIC is -2 log-likelihood + 2 x (number of parameters). Each additional cluster adds one allele frequency per locus and an ancestry proportion for every individual, so a cluster lowers AIC if it increases the log-likelihood by more than the number of loci plus the number of individuals:

Each point is a replicate, and the dashed line is the increase that a cluster needs to lower AIC. The second cluster (K=2), which separates the two populations, increases the log-likelihood far above the line with both treatments. Further clusters only fit noise. Declared, they gain little more than half of what AIC requires; undeclared, the noise of the pseudohaploids counts twice, and every further cluster passes the line.

Cross-validation is unaffected by the inflated log-likelihood

Cross-validation (Alexander & Lange 2011) holds out a fold of the genotypes, fits the model to the remaining ones, and scores how well it predicts the held-out genotypes. A cluster that fits only noise does not improve these predictions, so the cross-validation error stops decreasing at the true K, whatever the size of the log-likelihood:

Each line is a replicate, and the large points mark the K with the lowest error. The number of replicates in which each criterion picks each K:

K with the lowest AIC and cross-validation error, shown as “K (number of replicates)”, out of 5 replicates. The true K is 2.
Scenario Pseudohaploids Best K by AIC Best K by cross-validation
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.1 Undeclared 6 (5) 2 (5)
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.1 Declared 2 (5) 2 (5)
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.05 Undeclared 6 (5) 1 (5)
Pseudohaploids in A, F_ST = 0.05 Declared 2 (5) 2 (5)
B only pseudohaploids, F_ST = 0.1 Undeclared 6 (5) 2 (5)
B only pseudohaploids, F_ST = 0.1 Declared 2 (5) 2 (5)

With moderate structure (F_ST = 0.1), cross-validation picks the true K with both treatments, whereas AIC picks the largest K tested when the pseudohaploids are undeclared.

The cross-validation errors themselves are much larger when the pseudohaploids are undeclared (note the different scales of the plot): each held-out pseudohaploid genotype is scored as two copies of the same allele, which a diploid prediction rarely expects. The errors can only be compared between values of K of the same analysis, not between analyses that treat the pseudohaploids differently (e.g. ADMIXTURE and gt_radmix() on declared pseudohaploids).

Cross-validation picks too few clusters when the structure is weak

With weaker structure (F_ST = 0.05), cross-validation picks K = 1 when the pseudohaploids are undeclared, missing the two populations, and K = 2 when they are declared. At K = 2, the allele frequencies of the cluster of population A are a compromise between its diploids, which carry heterozygotes, and its undeclared pseudohaploids, which do not (see Ancestry proportions at the true K). The model then predicts the held-out genotypes of the pseudohaploids worse than at K = 1, where a single cluster cannot explain the lack of heterozygotes anyway, and its allele frequencies are simply those of the whole sample. These errors count twice, and when the structure is weak they outweigh the gain from separating the two populations. (We checked this by splitting the cross-validation error by group of individuals, in the first replicate of each design.)

To see when this happens, we simulated 20 diploids from each population, with 0 to 80 pseudohaploids from population A, for three values of F_ST, and compared the cross-validation errors of K = 1 and K = 2 (5 replicates of each combination):

Number of replicates in which cross-validation prefers K = 2 (the true K) to K = 1, with 20 diploids from each population and 0 to 80 pseudohaploids from population A.
Pseudohaploids Number of pseudohaploids F_ST = 0.03 F_ST = 0.05 F_ST = 0.1
Undeclared 0 0/5 0/5 5/5
Undeclared 20 0/5 0/5 5/5
Undeclared 40 0/5 0/5 5/5
Undeclared 80 0/5 5/5 5/5
Declared 0 0/5 0/5 5/5
Declared 20 0/5 1/5 5/5
Declared 40 0/5 5/5 5/5
Declared 80 0/5 5/5 5/5

At F_ST = 0.03, cross-validation misses the structure even without pseudohaploids, and at F_ST = 0.1 it always finds it. At the intermediate value, declared pseudohaploids add information, and 40 of them are enough for cross-validation to detect the two populations in every replicate. When undeclared, 20 or 40 pseudohaploids hide the structure. With 80, cross-validation finds it again: the cluster of population A then fits its pseudohaploids, which make up most of it (its diploids appear admixed instead), and at K = 1 the allele frequencies of the whole sample, dominated by population A, predict population B poorly. Whether undeclared pseudohaploids hide weak structure thus depends on the composition of the sample.

Too many clusters: ghost clusters among the pseudohaploids

Ancestry is often shown for a range of K, including values larger than the one picked by cross-validation, and AIC picks the largest K tested when the pseudohaploids are undeclared. Beyond the true K, the extra clusters split the populations into arbitrary groups, which fit the noise of the sample. When a population is known only from pseudohaploids, where these “ghost” clusters fall depends on whether the pseudohaploids are declared. In the first replicate of that scenario (20 diploids from population A and 40 pseudohaploids from population B):

Declared, the 20 diploids of population A and the 40 pseudohaploids of population B carry the same number of allele copies per locus (40). The first ghost cluster splits population B, which has more individuals, but the following ones are shared between the two populations. Undeclared, all the ghost clusters fall within population B, splitting the pseudohaploids into groups that do not exist, whereas population A remains a single cluster. Each ghost cluster lets some of the pseudohaploids have more extreme allele frequencies, which explains part of their lack of heterozygotes, and its gain counts twice.

Over all the replicates, we measure how many clusters each population is spread over by the effective number of clusters, 1 / sum_k m_k^2, where m_k is the mean ancestry of the population from cluster k. It is 1 for a population assigned to a single cluster, and K for a population spread evenly over K clusters:

Each point is a replicate, and the lines join the means. The dashed line marks K - 1 clusters, i.e. all clusters but one. Undeclared, in every replicate, the pseudohaploid population is spread over almost all the clusters but one, and the diploid population stays in that one; declared, the two populations share the ghost clusters from K = 4. An analysis with undeclared pseudohaploids would suggest structure among the ancient samples, and none in the modern ones, when neither has any.

Recommendations

Based on these results, we recommend the following:

  • Declare pseudohaploids with gt_pseudohaploid() before running gt_radmix(), and check the result with indiv_ploidy(). A diploid is only mistaken for a pseudohaploid if it has no heterozygous genotype among the loci tested (test_n_loci, 10,000 by default).
  • Do not choose K from the log-likelihood (e.g. with AIC, or by looking for the point where it stops increasing) when pseudohaploids might not be declared, or in programs that cannot declare them. Cross-validation is more robust, but can still miss weak structure.
  • Compare log-likelihoods and cross-validation errors only between analyses that treat the pseudohaploids in the same way.
  • With programs that treat every individual as diploid, expect the diploids of populations with many pseudohaploids to appear slightly admixed, and be wary of clusters beyond the best K that only split pseudohaploids.

How the replicated simulations were run

The replicated simulations are run with the script vignettes/articles/code/pseudohaploid_runs.R (in the source code of the package), which saves its results in vignettes/articles/data/pseudohaploids; this article reads them from there. The code below is taken from that script. It uses the simulator described in Simulating the data:

library(tidygenclust)
library(tidypopgen)
source("code/pseudohaploid_simulation.R")
start_time <- Sys.time()
out_dir <- "data/pseudohaploids"
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
# each replicate simulates a dataset with its own seed (also used for the
# fits), so every dataset can be simulated again on its own
replicates <- 1:5
n_cores <- min(4L, parallel::detectCores())

Each dataset is analysed for each K, with cross-validation (5 folds), with its pseudohaploids undeclared and declared:

# Analyse a dataset for each value of k, with cross-validation, twice: with
# the pseudohaploids undeclared (treated as diploids) and declared with
# gt_pseudohaploid(). Returns the log-likelihood and cross-validation error
# of each fit (fits), and, if with_q is TRUE, the ancestry proportions of
# each individual for each k > 1 (q, in long format)
analyse <- function(gt, k, seed, with_q = FALSE) {
  fits <- list()
  q <- list()
  for (treatment in c("undeclared", "declared")) {
    x <- if (treatment == "declared") gt_pseudohaploid(gt) else gt
    adm <- gt_radmix(
      x,
      k = k,
      seed = seed,
      crossval = TRUE,
      n_cores = n_cores
    )
    fits[[treatment]] <- data.frame(
      treatment = treatment,
      k = adm$k,
      loglik = adm$loglik,
      cv = adm$cv
    )
    if (with_q) {
      for (i in which(adm$k > 1)) {
        q_i <- unclass(adm$Q[[i]])
        q[[paste(treatment, i)]] <- data.frame(
          treatment = treatment,
          k = adm$k[i],
          id = gt$id,
          population = gt$population,
          type = gt$type,
          cluster = rep(seq_len(ncol(q_i)), each = nrow(q_i)),
          q = round(as.vector(q_i), 4)
        )
      }
    }
  }
  list(fits = do.call(rbind, fits), q = do.call(rbind, q))
}

The three scenarios are analysed for K = 1 to 6:

# three scenarios, all with 5,000 loci and two populations (so the true K is
# 2): pseudohaploids in one of the two populations, with moderate (F_ST =
# 0.1) or weak (F_ST = 0.05) structure; and a population known only from
# pseudohaploids (e.g. ancient samples), next to a diploid population
scenarios <- list(
  pseudohaploids_in_a = list(
    n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 20), n_pseudohaploid = c(A = 40), fst = 0.1
  ),
  weak_structure = list(
    n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 20), n_pseudohaploid = c(A = 40), fst = 0.05
  ),
  b_pseudohaploid = list(
    n_diploid = c(A = 20), n_pseudohaploid = c(B = 40), fst = 0.1
  )
)
# each scenario is analysed for K = 1 to 6
fits <- list()
q <- list()
for (scenario in names(scenarios)) {
  for (replicate in replicates) {
    message("Scenario ", scenario, ", replicate ", replicate)
    s <- scenarios[[scenario]]
    gt <- simulate_pseudohaploids(
      n_diploid = s$n_diploid,
      n_pseudohaploid = s$n_pseudohaploid,
      fst = s$fst,
      seed = replicate
    )
    res <- analyse(gt, k = 1:6, seed = replicate, with_q = TRUE)
    run <- paste(scenario, replicate)
    fits[[run]] <- data.frame(scenario, replicate, res$fits)
    q[[run]] <- data.frame(scenario, replicate, res$q)
  }
}
fits <- do.call(rbind, fits)
q <- do.call(rbind, q)

the grid of conditions for K = 1 and 2 only:

# when does cross-validation prefer K = 2 over K = 1? 20 diploids from each
# population, and 0 to 80 pseudohaploids from population A, with weak to
# moderate structure (K = 1 and 2 only)
grid <- expand.grid(
  fst = c(0.03, 0.05, 0.1),
  n_pseudohaploid = c(0, 20, 40, 80),
  replicate = replicates
)
grid_fits <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
  message("Grid ", i, " of ", nrow(grid))
  gt <- simulate_pseudohaploids(
    n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 20),
    n_pseudohaploid = c(A = grid$n_pseudohaploid[i]),
    fst = grid$fst[i],
    seed = grid$replicate[i]
  )
  res <- analyse(gt, k = 1:2, seed = grid$replicate[i])
  grid_fits[[i]] <- data.frame(grid[i, ], res$fits, row.names = NULL)
}
grid_fits <- do.call(rbind, grid_fits)

and the designs with populations of different sizes, at K = 2, with the allele frequencies estimated or fixed at their true values:

# why do the individuals of the larger population appear slightly admixed
# at K = 2? Two populations of different or equal sizes, with or without
# pseudohaploids, fitted at K = 2 with the allele frequencies estimated (with
# the pseudohaploids undeclared and declared), and with the allele
# frequencies fixed at their true values (pseudohaploids declared)
sample_size_designs <- list(
  equal = list(n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 20), n_pseudohaploid = c()),
  a_larger = list(n_diploid = c(A = 60, B = 20), n_pseudohaploid = c()),
  pseudohaploids_in_a = list(
    n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 20), n_pseudohaploid = c(A = 40)
  ),
  b_larger = list(n_diploid = c(A = 20, B = 60), n_pseudohaploid = c(A = 40))
)
# more replicates than above, as the differences are small
sample_size_replicates <- 1:10
sample_size <- list()
for (design in names(sample_size_designs)) {
  for (replicate in sample_size_replicates) {
    message("Design ", design, ", replicate ", replicate)
    d <- sample_size_designs[[design]]
    gt <- simulate_pseudohaploids(
      n_diploid = d$n_diploid,
      n_pseudohaploid = d$n_pseudohaploid,
      fst = 0.1,
      seed = replicate
    )
    fit <- function(x, frequencies) {
      adm <- gt_radmix(
        x,
        k = 2,
        seed = replicate,
        n_cores = n_cores,
        init_p = if (frequencies == "true") attr(gt, "frequencies"),
        fix_p = frequencies == "true"
      )
      q_i <- unclass(adm$Q[[1]])
      # the cluster of each population: with the true frequencies, the
      # column of the population; otherwise, the cluster with the largest
      # mean ancestry among its individuals
      own <- if (frequencies == "true") {
        c(A = 1, B = 2)
      } else {
        sapply(c(A = "A", B = "B"), function(pop) {
          unname(which.max(colMeans(q_i[gt$population == pop, ])))
        })
      }
      own <- own[gt$population]
      # the mean ancestry of each group from the other cluster
      other <- 1 - q_i[cbind(seq_len(nrow(q_i)), own)]
      data.frame(
        design = design,
        replicate = replicate,
        frequencies = frequencies,
        stats::aggregate(
          list(other = other),
          list(population = gt$population, type = gt$type),
          mean
        )
      )
    }
    runs <- list(
      fit(gt_pseudohaploid(gt), "estimated"),
      fit(gt_pseudohaploid(gt), "true")
    )
    runs[[1]]$treatment <- runs[[2]]$treatment <- "declared"
    if (length(d$n_pseudohaploid) > 0) {
      runs[[3]] <- fit(gt, "estimated")
      runs[[3]]$treatment <- "undeclared"
    }
    sample_size[[paste(design, replicate)]] <- do.call(rbind, runs)
  }
}
sample_size <- do.call(rbind, sample_size)

To run the simulations again (e.g. after changing tidygenclust), install tidygenclust with R CMD INSTALL, rather than loading it with devtools::load_all(), which compiles its C++ code without optimisation, and run, from vignettes/articles:

cd vignettes/articles
Rscript code/pseudohaploid_runs.R

This takes about half an hour on 4 cores. Then render this article again.
